summary.text: Beta decay is a type of radioactive decay in which an atomic nucleus emits a beta particle, which is a fast energetic electron or positron.
In beta minus decay a neutron is converted to a proton, and in beta plus decay a proton is converted to a neutron.
It lets unstable atoms reach a more stable ratio of protons to neutrons, and the original element becomes a new chemical element.

facts.label: Force behind it
facts.value: The weak force, which has relatively long decay times

facts.label: Beta minus change
facts.value: Atomic number rises by one; mass number stays the same

facts.label: Other name
facts.value: Beta plus decay is also called positron emission

facts.label: Particle origin
facts.value: The beta particle is created in the decay, not stored beforehand

facts.label: Neutrino clue
facts.value: Studying beta decay gave the first physical evidence for the neutrino

items.prompt: Inside an unstable nucleus, a neutron converts into a proton. What does the process also create?

options.label: An electron and an electron antineutrino
A positron and an electron neutrino
An electron and an electron neutrino
A positron and an electron antineutrino

items.explain: In beta minus decay a neutron is converted to a proton, and the process creates an electron and an electron antineutrino.

items.prompt: Carbon-14 turns into nitrogen-14 by beta minus decay. How do its mass number and atomic number change?

options.label: Mass number rises by one and atomic number stays the same
Both numbers fall by one
Mass number stays the same and atomic number rises by one
Mass number falls by four and atomic number falls by two

items.explain: The new element has an unchanged mass number but an atomic number increased by one.

items.prompt: A student says the electron in beta decay was waiting inside the nucleus until it escaped. What is wrong with that?

options.label: The electron was actually stored in the outer shells of the atom
The electron is created in the decay and does not exist in the nucleus beforehand
The electron was inside, but only as a pair with a positron
The electron was waiting inside the nucleus as part of a neutron

items.explain: Neither the beta particle nor its associated neutrino exists within the nucleus prior to beta decay; they are created in the decay process.

items.prompt: A nucleus emits an electron in beta decay. Why must an antineutrino come out as well?

options.label: A neutrino is needed to carry away the nucleus's charge
Antineutrinos are needed to slow the electron down
Electrons cannot leave a nucleus without a partner of the same kind
The electron's lepton number of +1 needs an antiparticle at −1 to balance it

items.explain: Beta decay conserves lepton number; protons and neutrons have lepton number zero, so an electron must be accompanied by an electron antineutrino.

items.prompt: In a beta minus decay, the electron is measured with less than the full energy released. Where does the rest go?

options.label: It is shared between the antineutrino and the recoiling nuclide
It stays in the nucleus as stored energy
It is carried off by a second electron
It disappears, as energy is lost in this decay

items.explain: The total energy of the decay is divided between the electron, the antineutrino and the recoiling nuclide, so the beta spectrum is continuous.

items.prompt: Rutherford sorted radioactive emissions by how well they pass through metal. Which result matches what he found?

options.label: Both kinds were stopped at once by thin paper
Beta rays were stopped by thin sheets while alpha rays went through aluminium
A thin sheet stopped alpha rays, but beta rays passed several millimetres of aluminium
Both kinds passed through aluminium in just the same way

items.explain: Alpha rays could be stopped by thin sheets of paper or aluminium, whereas beta rays could penetrate several millimetres of aluminium.
